notes: Fundamental factual error in permitted development calculations; RSC 94.13(7) mandatory remittal despite withdrawal plan.

enrichment.short_title: Leeds CC v SSHD: enforcement notice appeal on false PDR premise
key_facts: Leeds City Council served an enforcement notice requiring demolition of unauthorised dormers and an extension at 61 High Ash Avenue, calculated on assumed 70 cubic metre permitted development rights.
The inspector varied the notice substituting 105 cubic metres but upheld it; the council later discovered permitted development rights were effectively exhausted.
The council accepted the notice was issued on a false premise and undertook to withdraw it within 14 days.
Sullivan J held the inspector's decision was erroneous in law because of the fundamental factual error but was constrained by RSC Order 94.13(7) to remit to the Secretary of State.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 289 appeal to the High Court against an inspector's decision on an enforcement notice appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and matter remitted to the Secretary of State, with no redetermination for at least 14 days pending withdrawal; council ordered to pay the Secretary of State's costs of £3,158.
enrichment.ratio: A fundamental error of fact underlying an enforcement notice and inspector's decision may constitute an error of law as irrelevant or omitted relevant considerations, but RSC 94.13(7) still requires remittal rather than quashing where the court finds legal error.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector erred in calculating permitted development rights
Whether a fundamental factual error amounts to an error of law on appeal
Effect of RSC Order 94.13(7) where remittal would serve no practical purpose
Appropriate order where the council intends to withdraw the enforcement notice

notes: MDMA conspiracy conviction and sentence appeals refused; confiscation equity valuation principle affirmed.

enrichment.short_title: Mouldon: MDMA conspiracy, sentence and confiscation appeals refused
key_facts: Mouldon was convicted by a majority of conspiracy to supply MDMA following an undercover operation at Ace Hardware Store in Newcastle.
Telephone and CCTV evidence linked him as Wilson's supplier of large quantities of ecstasy; he was sentenced to 16 years' imprisonment.
A confiscation order of £667,000 realisable assets was made with a benefit finding of at least £750,000.
Properties had been acquired using drug proceeds together with mortgage finance that increased in value before confiscation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against conviction and sentence, and application for leave to appeal against a confiscation order under the Drug Trafficking Act 1994.
enrichment.outcome: All applications refused; payment time for the confiscation order extended by three months.
enrichment.ratio: Under the Drug Trafficking Act 1994 the benefit from drug trafficking is the value of property acquired with proceeds, valued at the confiscation date subject to charges, not merely the original cash deposit; section 4 assumptions apply to equity in mortgaged property.
legal_issues: Whether the judge's summing-up was biased against the applicant
Whether a 16-year sentence was manifestly excessive given prior class B convictions
Whether confiscation benefit should be limited to the proportion of property represented by drug-derived deposits
Application of sections 4 and 7 where mortgaged property appreciates in value

notes: Split outcome on Saudi torture claims: state immunity upheld for Kingdom; individual officials not cloaked by ratione materiae immunity.

enrichment.short_title: Jones v Saudi Arabia: torture claims, state immunity and individual officials
key_facts: Ronald Jones alleged systematic torture during 67 days' Saudi detention after a Riyadh bomb blast; Mitchell, Walker and Sampson brought parallel claims against Saudi police and Interior Ministry officials.
Saudi Arabia applied to set aside service on state immunity grounds following Al-Adsani v United Kingdom.
The Court of Appeal distinguished immunity ratione personae enjoyed by the Kingdom from immunity ratione materiae for individual torturers.
Jones's claim against the Kingdom was struck out, but service-out applications against individual defendants were remitted to the master.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals from a master's decisions on state immunity, service out of the jurisdiction and alternative service in tort claims alleging torture in Saudi Arabia.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal against dismissal of Jones's claim against the Kingdom dismissed; appeals allowing reconsideration of service against individual defendants in both claims allowed and remitted to the master.
enrichment.ratio: Following Al-Adsani, Saudi Arabia retains state immunity ratione personae from civil torture claims, but individual officials are not protected by the state's ratione materiae immunity where torture is not a matter of state conduct; Propend does not extend immunity to such individual claims.
legal_issues: Whether torture claims against a foreign state are barred by the State Immunity Act 1978
Whether UNCAT Article 14 creates an exception to state immunity for civil reparation
Whether Saudi officials share the Kingdom's immunity under section 14(1)
Distinction between immunity ratione personae and ratione materiae after Pinochet and Al-Adsani
linked_authorities: R v Bow Street Metropolitan Stipendiary Magistrate, Ex parte Pinochet (No 3) [2000] 1 AC 147
Propend Finance Property Ltd v Sing [1997] 1 WLR 637

notes: Disqualified juror on probation held not to render majority rape convictions unsafe under Juries Act section 18.

enrichment.short_title: Richardson: disqualified juror and safety of rape convictions
key_facts: Richardson was convicted by 10:2 majorities of six counts of rape and one indecent assault on a complainant aged 12 to 16.
Juror Mr Zaman had pleaded guilty to indecent assault and vagrancy offences and was subject to a community rehabilitation order when he sat, but no further PNC check was made after deferral.
The juror did not disclose his disqualification despite leaflet warnings; he was on the sex offenders register.
No complaint was made about trial conduct; the sole ground was the juror's disqualification under Schedule 1 Part II.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for leave to appeal against conviction referred to the full Court of Appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to appeal granted but appeal dismissed; convictions held safe despite the disqualified juror.
enrichment.ratio: Section 18 of the Juries Act 1974 bars overturning a verdict merely because a juror was disqualified unless there is evidence or a proper inference of prejudice or an unsafe trial; majority verdicts and the nature of the juror's offences did not make these convictions unsafe.
legal_issues: Effect of section 18 Juries Act 1974 on appeals based on juror disqualification
Whether a majority verdict is unsafe if a disqualified juror may have been in the majority
Application of Bliss, Chapman and Salt to probation-disqualified jurors
Whether the juror's sexual offence convictions necessarily undermined trial fairness
linked_authorities: R v Bliss (1986) 84 Cr App R 1
R v Chapman and Lauday (1976) 63 Cr App R 75

notes: Construction adjudication enforcement appeal allowed; no apparent bias in Biscoe's second decision on same dispute.

enrichment.short_title: AMEC v Whitefriars: adjudicator bias and jurisdiction in construction dispute

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: AMEC claimed about £508,000 unpaid after Whitefriars terminated a JCT letter-of-intent contract for Tudor Street works.
Adjudicator Michael Biscoe awarded payment in a first adjudication later held a nullity for wrong appointment; RIBA re-nominated Biscoe for a second adjudication.
Whitefriars resisted enforcement alleging lack of jurisdiction and breaches of natural justice including apparent bias.
Judge Toulmin QC refused enforcement; the Court of Appeal held clause 39A.3 did not apply before any adjudicator was appointed and rejected bias arguments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal to enforce a construction adjudicator's decision under the 1996 Act scheme.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; adjudicator's decision enforced with costs and payment orders; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 39A.3 replacement machinery applies only after an adjudicator has been appointed under clause 39A.2; reappointment of the same adjudicator on the same dispute does not of itself establish apparent bias under Porter v Magill, and natural justice does not require parties to be heard on an adjudicator's powerless jurisdiction decision.
legal_issues: Correct contractual route to appoint an adjudicator after death of the named adjudicator
Whether re-nominating the same adjudicator gave rise to apparent bias
Effect of prior legal advice obtained in the first adjudication
Whether natural justice requires consultation before an adjudicator proceeds despite a jurisdiction challenge
linked_authorities: Locabail (UK) Ltd v Bayfield Properties Ltd [2000] QB 451
Discain Project Services Ltd v Opecprime Development Ltd [2000] BLR 402

notes: Asylum accommodation centre: Circular 18/84 NPD procedure held lawful alternative to section 299 where development is on behalf of Crown.

enrichment.short_title: Cherwell DC v SSHD: Circular 18/84 procedure for asylum accommodation centre
key_facts: The Home Office proposed a 750-place asylum seeker accommodation centre on former MoD land at Piddington near Bicester under a design-build-operate contract.
Cherwell District Council objected; a non-statutory public inquiry under DOE Circular 18/84 approved the development despite the inspector's recommendation against it.
The council challenged use of the Notice of Proposed Development procedure instead of a section 299 planning application.
A section 299A planning obligation agreement imposed development conditions enforceable against the DBO contractor.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review appeal (permission limited to ground 1) against approval of Crown development under Circular 18/84 Part IV.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; use of the NPD procedure held not an abuse of power where development would be carried out on behalf of the Crown and section 294(1) would prevent ordinary enforcement in any event.
enrichment.ratio: The Crown may choose Circular 18/84 consultation rather than section 299 even for DBO projects; development by a private contractor on Crown land can be 'on behalf of the Crown' for section 294(1), and statutory enforcement would remain unavailable whether or not section 299 permission were obtained.
legal_issues: Whether the Home Office was obliged to use section 299 rather than Circular 18/84
Whether DBO contractor development on a Crown lease is development by or on behalf of the Crown
Equivalence of safeguards and enforcement between NPD approval and statutory planning permission
Effect of section 294(1) immunity on the council's enforcement concerns

Lord Advocate v Dumbarton District Council [1990] 2 AC 580
London Borough of Hillingdon v Secretary of State (unreported, 30 July 1999)

notes: Attorney General's reference: night-time group robbery sentence increased from 30 months to 4 years YOI.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref 98/2004: unduly lenient night-time kiosk robbery
key_facts: An 18-year-old offender pleaded guilty to robbery and assault occasioning ABH after attacking Mr Prince at a Pendleton telephone kiosk at night.
CCTV showed a group of four youths punching, kicking and stamping on the victim before and after stealing cash, a phone and lighters.
The recorder sentenced him to 30 months on robbery and 12 months concurrent on ABH despite describing the footage as shocking.
The offender had prior youth cautions and a conditional discharge for carrying a bladed article.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging unduly lenient sentences.
enrichment.outcome: Reference upheld; robbery sentence increased to 4 years' detention in a young offender institution with double jeopardy adjustment; concurrent ABH sentence unchanged.
enrichment.ratio: Group night-time robbery with shod-foot violence exceeding that needed for theft and gratuitous post-robbery assault warrants a sentence at the upper end of the 18-month to 5-year bracket; 30 months failed to reflect aggravating features and public concern.
legal_issues: Whether 30 months was unduly lenient for robbery with significant gratuitous violence
Relevance of group offending, night-time location and use of shod feet as weapons
Application of sentencing bracket in Attorney General's References Nos 4 and 7 of 2002
Mitigating effect of first-available guilty plea and youth
linked_authorities: R v Gordon & Foster [2001] 1 Cr App R(S) 200
Attorney General's References Nos 4 and 7 of 2002 [2002] 2 Cr App R(S) 345

notes: Murder appeals dismissed; telephone and movement evidence sufficient for no-case-to-answer ruling.

enrichment.short_title: Mullings and Morgan: murder no-case-to-answer and telephone evidence
key_facts: Shakir Ali died from a stab wound and massive beating after three assailants arrived at his Walthamstow flat on 4 July 2001.
Smallon had earlier threatened revenge after a Selborne Road confrontation; his Fiat Bravo was linked to the killing.
Telephone cell-site evidence showed Mullings and Morgan travelling from separate locations to Walthamstow and converging near Smallon's home before and after the attack.
Musawar Ali identified Mullings and Morgan at parades, but identifications were weak alone; both denied presence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals against conviction for murder following refusal of no-case-to-answer submissions at trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; judge correctly left the case to the jury given combined telephone, movement and contextual evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Weak identification evidence may support a murder conviction when combined with telephone contact patterns and coordinated journeys before and after the killing; fresh evidence of other possible enemies was peripheral and would not have affected the defence.
legal_issues: Whether there was a case to answer against Mullings and Morgan on murder
Admissibility and weight of cell-site telephone evidence
Whether Smallon's involvement evidence was admissible against co-defendants
Whether proposed fresh evidence under section 23 should be admitted

notes: Brief post-judgment ruling refusing to reopen AMEC adjudication appeal on Scheme paragraph 9(2) point.

enrichment.short_title: AMEC v Whitefriars: refusal to reopen appeal on Scheme para 9(2)
key_facts: At the judgment hand-down in AMEC v Whitefriars ([2004] EWCA Civ 1418), new counsel for Whitefriars raised paragraph 9(2) of the adjudication scheme.
The point had not been argued at trial or on the main appeal.
Counsel invited the court to reopen the appeal to consider whether inconsistent adjudicator findings were barred.
Chadwick and Dyson LJJ held the paragraph avoids inconsistent findings by different adjudicators, not where the first decision was a nullity.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application at judgment hand-down to adjourn and reopen the adjudication enforcement appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application to adjourn and reopen refused; paragraph 9(2) held inapplicable where the first adjudicator's decision was a nullity.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 9(2) of the Scheme prevents inconsistent findings on the same issue by different adjudicators but does not apply when an earlier adjudication decision is treated as never having been made because it lacked jurisdiction.
legal_issues: Whether the court should reopen a concluded appeal for a new point on paragraph 9(2)
Scope of paragraph 9(2) where a prior adjudication decision is a nullity
Effect of a second adjudicator determining the same dispute after jurisdictional invalidity of the first decision

notes: Conspiracy to rob conviction quashed for exclusion of psychologist's duress evidence; retrial refused.

enrichment.short_title: Antar: robbery conspiracy, PACE interview and duress expert evidence
key_facts: Antar and Aidoo were convicted of conspiracy to rob three men at a bus stop in Wickham Lane in October 2002.
Antar was interviewed without caution or an appropriate adult and denied involvement, but at trial admitted the robbery under duress from Rashid Jagun.
Dr McAnena's evidence of IQ 51, learning disability and high suggestibility was ruled inadmissible after a voir dire.
The judge refused severance; Aidoo cross-examined Antar using the taped interview on his changed account.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction for conspiracy to rob by leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction quashed as unsafe because psychologist evidence relevant to the objective duress test was wrongly excluded; retrial refused given time served and pending kidnapping proceedings.
enrichment.ratio: Expert evidence of mental impairment or learning disability and elevated suggestibility is admissible on the objective limb of the duress test under Bowen; excluding such evidence where the jury should assess reasonable firmness with those characteristics renders a conviction unsafe.
legal_issues: Admissibility of an uncautioned PACE interview used only in cross-examination by a co-defendant
Whether joint trial with Aidoo was an abuse of process
Admissibility of psychological evidence on duress where IQ is extremely low
Whether a retrial was in the public interest
linked_authorities: R v Bowen [1996] 2 Cr App R 157
